refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: udev supplies the system software with device events, manages permissions of device nodes and may create additional symlinks in the /dev/ directory, or renames network interfaces. The kernel usually just assigns unpredictable device names based on the order of discovery. Meaningful symlinks or network device names provide a way to reliably identify devices based on their properties or current configuration.

The udev daemon, systemd-udevd.service8, receives device uevents directly from the kernel whenever a device is added or removed from the system, or it changes its state. When udev receives a device event, it matches its configured set of rules against various device attributes to identify the device. Rules that match may provide additional device information to be stored in the udev database or to be used to create meaningful symlink names.
All device information udev processes is stored in the udev database and sent out to possible event subscribers. Access to all stored data and the event sources is provided by the library libudev.

refsect1.title: Rules Files
refsect1.para: The udev rules are read from the files located in the system rules directories /usr/lib/udev/rules.d and /usr/local/lib/udev/rules.d, the volatile runtime directory /run/udev/rules.d and the local administration directory /etc/udev/rules.d. All rules files are collectively sorted and processed in lexicographic order, regardless of the directories in which they live. However, files with identical filenames replace each other. Files in /etc/ have the highest priority, files in /run/ take precedence over files with the same name under /usr/. This can be used to override a system-supplied rules file with a local file if needed; a symlink in /etc/ with the same name as a rules file in /usr/lib/, pointing to /dev/null, disables the rules file entirely. Rule files must have the extension .rules; other extensions are ignored.

Rules files are line-based text files. Each line contains at most one rule, which consists of one or more tokens (see below). A line ending with a backslash (\) is joined with the following line, and the result is processed as a single line. Lines beginning with # are ignored, even within a continuation. An empty or whitespace-only line ends a pending continuation and is otherwise ignored.

refsect1.title: Rule Syntax
refsect1.para: A rule consists of a comma-separated list of one or more tokens (key-operator-value expressions). Each token has a distinct effect, depending on the key and operator used. A rule may contain both matching and assigning tokens: the assignments are applied only if all matches succeed.

refsect2.title: Lines and Tokens
refsect2.para: The general format of a token is:
with the following parts:

listitem.para: One of the key names described in the Match Keys and Assignments sections below, for example KERNEL or SYMLINK. The key determines what is matched against or assigned.

An optional key-specific argument, enclosed in braces. For example, ENV{property} takes a property name, ATTR{sysfs attribute} takes a sysfs attribute name, IMPORT{type} takes an import type, and TEST{mask} takes an octal file mode mask. Keys that do not take an attribute must not be given one.
One of ==, !=, =, :=, += or -=; see Operators below. Not every key accepts every operator; the allowed operators are listed for each key.
An optional prefix attached to the value: e for C-style escaped strings and i for case-insensitive matching; see Values below.

The value to match against or assign, written as a double-quoted string; see Values below. Depending on the key, the value is interpreted as a pattern (see Pattern Matching) and may contain string substitutions (see String Substitutions).

refsect2.para: For example, in the rule
the first two tokens are matches (on the subsystem and on a sysfs attribute), and the third token assigns the interface name. The interface is only renamed if both matches succeed.

Tokens are separated by commas, optionally surrounded by whitespace. Although tokens may be written in any order, they are evaluated in a fixed internal order, determined by the key: all match keys are evaluated before all assignment keys, regardless of where they appear in the rule. The full order and its consequences are described in Token Processing Order below.

refsect2.title: Token Processing Order
refsect2.para: The tokens of a rule are evaluated in the following order, determined by the key. Tokens with the same key and attribute are evaluated in the order they are specified. The assignments are applied only if all matches succeed.

listitem.para: The plain match keys: ACTION, DEVPATH, KERNEL, SYMLINK, NAME, ENV, CONST, TAG, SUBSYSTEM, DRIVER, ATTR, and SYSCTL
The parent device match keys: KERNELS, SUBSYSTEMS, DRIVERS, ATTRS, and TAGS, evaluated together while walking up the device chain (see Matching Parent Devices below)
OWNER, GROUP, and MODE

refsect2.para: This order has several consequences:

listitem.para: No match key can see properties assigned in the same rule.
RESULT is evaluated after all PROGRAM keys of the rule, so it is matched against the output of the last executed program.

Properties imported by IMPORT{} are visible to all assignments of the rule, while properties assigned by ENV are visible only to the assignments that follow it in the order above: NAME, SYMLINK, ATTR, SYSCTL, and RUN.
The OPTIONS string-escape settings affect the NAME, SYMLINK, and ENV assignments of the same rule.
Compare for equality: the specified key has the specified value. The value may be a pattern; see Pattern Matching below.
Compare for inequality: the specified key does not have the specified value or the specified key is not present at all. The value may be a pattern.
Assign a value to a key. Keys that represent a list are reset and only this single value is assigned.
Add the value to a key that holds a list of entries.
Remove the value from a key that holds a list of entries.
Assign a value to a key finally; disallow any later changes.

refsect2.title: Values
refsect2.para: Values are written as double-quoted strings, such as '"string"'. To include a quotation mark (") in the value, precede it by a backslash, i.e. '\"'. Any other occurrences of a backslash followed by a character are not unescaped. That is, \t\n is treated as four characters: backslash, lowercase t, backslash, lowercase n.

The string can be prefixed with a lowercase e to mark the string as C-style escaped, see Escape sequences in C. For example, 'e"string\n"' is parsed as 7 characters: 6 lowercase letters and a newline. This can be useful for writing special characters when a kernel driver requires them.

The string can be prefixed with a lowercase i to mark that the string or pattern will match case-insensitively. For example, 'i"foo"' will match foo, FOO, FoO, and so on. The prefix can be used only for match (==) or unmatch (!=) rules, e.g. ATTR{foo}==i"abcd". The e and i prefixes may be combined, in either order, e.g. 'ei"foo"'.
Please note that NUL is not allowed in either string variant.

refsect2.title: Pattern Matching
refsect2.para: The values of most match keys are interpreted as patterns: they support shell glob pattern matching and alternate patterns. This applies to the ACTION, DEVPATH, KERNEL, SUBSYSTEM, DRIVER, SYMLINK, NAME, ENV, CONST, TAG, ATTR, SYSCTL, KERNELS, SUBSYSTEMS, DRIVERS, ATTRS, TAGS, and RESULT match keys. The values of TEST, PROGRAM, and IMPORT are not patterns: they are file paths and command lines (the value of IMPORT{parent} is a single glob pattern matched against property names, and does not support alternate patterns). The following special characters are supported in patterns:

listitem.para: Matches zero or more characters.
Matches any single character.

Matches any single character specified within the brackets. For example, the pattern string tty[SR] would match either ttyS or ttyR. Ranges are also supported via the - character. For example, to match on the range of all digits, the pattern [0-9] could be used. If the first character following the [ is a !, any characters not enclosed are matched.
Separates alternative patterns. For example, the pattern string abc|x* would match either abc or x*.

refsect2.para: An empty alternative — produced by a leading, trailing, or doubled |, e.g. |foo — matches an unset or empty value. For example, ENV{FOO}=="bar|" matches when the property is set to bar or is unset or empty. To test that a value is set and non-empty, the patterns '=="?*"' and '!=""' are commonly used, e.g. ENV{FOO}=="?*". The ATTR and ATTRS keys are an exception: if the attribute cannot be read, the token is false regardless of the pattern, even with the != operator.
The SYMLINK and TAG match keys test a list of values (symlinks, tags); the token matches if any of the values matches. With the != operator, the token is true only if none of the values matches.
For SUBSYSTEM, the value subsystem matches the devices that represent the subsystem enumeration directories themselves.

refsect2.title: Referring to Other Devices
refsect2.para: Several keys and substitutions accept an attribute name in the following format, which addresses a specific device by its subsystem and kernel name instead of the event device:
For example, the sysfs attribute /sys/class/dmi/id/product_name can be matched with

The referenced device is looked up directly: the attribute is read from (or written to) it, regardless of the event device or its parents. Attribute names in this format are looked up literally by ATTR, ATTRS, and $attr{}: string substitutions are not applied to them. TEST is an exception: its path is substituted before the device reference is resolved, so e.g. TEST=="[net/$env{INTERFACE}]operstate" is supported.
The format is supported by the following keys and substitutions:

listitem.para: ATTR{attribute}, for both matching and assignment,
ATTRS{attribute} (the attribute is read from the referenced device instead of the devices along the devpath),
TEST (as a leading prefix of a relative path, resolved to the referenced device's sysfs path), and
the $attr{attribute} substitution.

refsect2.title: Key Overview
refsect2.para: The following tables summarize the keys, the attributes they take, the operators they accept, whether their match values are patterns, and where string substitutions are applied. See the next two sections for the detailed descriptions.
Match keys:
Assignment keys:

refsect1.title: Match Keys
refsect1.para: The following keys can be used to match against device properties. With the == and != operators, they decide whether the rule (and thus the assignments in it) is applied.

refsect2.title: Matching the Event Device
refsect2.para: These keys are matched against the event device itself:

listitem.para: Match the name of the event action, e.g. add or remove. See the Event Actions section for the list of actions and their meaning.
Match the devpath of the event device, e.g. /devices/pci0000:00/0000:00:14.0/usb1/1-2/1-2:1.0/ttyUSB0/tty/ttyUSB0.
Match the name assigned by the kernel to the event device, e.g. sda or ttyUSB0.
Match the subsystem of the event device, e.g. net or block.
Match the driver name of the event device. Only set this key for devices which are bound to a driver at the time the event is generated.

Match the name of a symlink targeting the device node, without the /dev/ prefix, e.g. disk/by-label/root. It can be used once a SYMLINK key has been set in one of the preceding rules. There may be multiple symlinks; only one needs to match. If the operator is !=, the token returns true only if there is no symlink matched.
Match the name of a network interface. It can be used once the NAME key has been set in one of the preceding rules.

Match against a device property value, e.g. properties set by the kernel (such as DEVTYPE or MODALIAS), imported by IMPORT{}, or assigned by earlier rules. An unset property is matched as the empty value; see Pattern Matching above.
Match against a system-wide constant. Supported keys are:
System's architecture. See ConditionArchitecture= in systemd.unit5 for possible values.
System's virtualization environment. See systemd-detect-virt1 for possible values.
System's confidential virtualization technology. See systemd-detect-virt1 for possible values.
Unknown keys will never match.

Match against one of device tags. It can be used once a TAG key has been set in one of the preceding rules. There may be multiple tags; only one needs to match. If the operator is !=, the token returns true only if there is no tag matched.

Match the value of a sysfs attribute of the event device, e.g. ATTR{address} for a network interface. The attribute name may be a relative path with / separators, e.g. ATTR{power/control}, and may also address another device with the [SUBSYSTEM/KERNEL]attribute format; see Referring to Other Devices above.
Trailing whitespace in the attribute values is ignored unless the specified match value itself contains trailing whitespace.
The attribute name supports string substitutions, unless it is specified in the [SUBSYSTEM/KERNEL]attribute format, which is looked up literally; see String Substitutions below.

Match the value of a kernel parameter (sysctl), e.g. SYSCTL{kernel/hostname}. Both / and . may be used as separators in the parameter name. The parameter name supports string substitutions; see String Substitutions below.

refsect2.title: Matching Parent Devices
refsect2.para: Devices are organized hierarchically in sysfs: every device except the root of its chain has a parent device (for example, a partition is a child of its disk, which is a child of the storage controller it is attached to). The following keys match against the devices along this chain:

listitem.para: Search the devpath upwards for a matching device name.
Search the devpath upwards for a matching device subsystem name.
Search the devpath upwards for a matching device driver name.

Search the devpath upwards for a device with a matching sysfs attribute value. Trailing whitespace in the attribute values is ignored unless the specified match value itself contains trailing whitespace. The attribute may also address another device with the [SUBSYSTEM/KERNEL]attribute format; see Referring to Other Devices above.

Referencing attributes through the device/ symlink or through ../ (e.g. ATTRS{device/serial} or ATTRS{../serial}) is discouraged: these paths may not be available in future kernels. Prefer matching the attribute of the parent device directly, as shown by udevadm info --attribute-walk.
Search the devpath upwards for a device with matching tag. If the operator is !=, the token returns true only if there is no tag matched.

refsect2.para: The search starts with the event device itself and continues towards the root of the device chain. If several parent match keys are specified in a single rule, all of them must match one and the same device in the chain (although different rules may match at different levels). If no device in the chain satisfies all parent match keys, the rule does not match.
both SUBSYSTEMS and ATTRS must match the same USB device, and $id expands to the kernel name of that USB device (e.g. 3-2).

refsect2.title: Matching Against Files and Program Results

listitem.para: Test the existence of a file. The value is a file path; if it is relative, it is taken relative to the sysfs path of the event device, unless it starts with a [SUBSYSTEM/KERNEL] prefix, which is resolved to that device's sysfs path (see Referring to Other Devices above). A /*/ sequence in the path is expanded: the * is replaced by the first non-hidden entry of the preceding directory for which the remainder of the path exists; only the first such sequence is expanded, and a * that is not a whole path component is taken literally. The value supports string substitutions, see String Substitutions below.

Optionally, an octal file mode mask may be specified as the attribute; the token then matches if the file exists and any of the bits set in the mask are also set in the file's mode. For example, the following rule matches block devices whose device node is writable by its owner:

Execute a program to determine whether there is a match; the key is true if the program returns successfully. The program's standard output is available in the RESULT key. How the command line is specified, and which restrictions apply to the executed program, are described in Program Execution below.

Multiple PROGRAM keys may be specified in one rule; they are executed sequentially, in the order they are specified, and the output of the last executed program is used for the RESULT match. As with any other match key, the remaining tokens of the rule are not evaluated once one of the programs fails. For example,

Match the returned string of the last PROGRAM call. This key can be used in the same or in any later rule after a PROGRAM call. If several PROGRAM keys were executed, the output of the most recently executed one is matched; see Token Processing Order above.

refsect1.title: Assignments
refsect1.para: The following keys can get values assigned. Assignments in a rule are only applied if all match keys of the rule succeed.

listitem.para: The name to use for a network interface. This key is only used to rename network interfaces; other devices — in particular device nodes — cannot be renamed by udev. The interface is renamed when the device is added; on other events, the assignment only affects the $name substitution and later NAME matches. Assigning %k or the empty string is rejected. See systemd.link5 for a higher-level mechanism for setting the interface name.

The name of a symlink targeting the device node, e.g. disk/by-id/usb-1234567890 for /dev/sda. With +=, the value is added to the list of symlinks to be created; with = or :=, the list is reset to this value; with -=, the value is removed from the list.

The set of characters to name a symlink is limited. Allowed characters are 0-9A-Za-z#+-.:=@_/, valid UTF-8 character sequences, and \x00 hex encoding. All other characters are replaced by a _ character.

Multiple symlinks may be specified by separating the names by the space character. In case multiple devices claim the same name, the link always points to the device with the highest link priority, set with the link_priority= option of OPTIONS (0 if unset). If the current device goes away, the links are re-evaluated and the device with the next highest link priority becomes the owner of the link. If several devices have the same priority, which one of them owns the link is undefined.
Symlink names must never conflict with the kernel's default device node names, as that would result in unpredictable behavior.

The permissions for the device node. Every specified value overrides the compiled-in default value. The user and group may be specified as a name or a numeric ID. Note that assigning a user or group that is not a system user or group is deprecated.
Applies the specified Linux Security Module label to the device node.

Set a device property value. With +=, the value is appended to the current value of the property, separated by a space; assigning the empty string removes the property. Properties that are set by the kernel or by udev itself (such as ACTION, DEVPATH, DEVNAME, DEVLINKS or INTERFACE) cannot be assigned or removed.
Property names with a leading . are neither stored in the database nor exported to events or external tools (run by, for example, the PROGRAM match key).

Attach a tag to a device. With +=, the tag is added to the current list of tags; with -=, the tag is removed from the current list of tags only — it remains in the stored TAGS property and in the tag index, so libudev monitor and enumeration filters still match it. With =, tags added by earlier rules during the current event are dropped, and the value is assigned.

This is used to filter events for users of libudev's monitor functionality, or to enumerate a group of tagged devices. The implementation can only work efficiently if only a few tags are attached to a device. It is only meant to be used in contexts with specific device filter requirements, and not as a general-purpose flag. Excessive use might result in inefficient event handling.

The value that should be written to a sysfs attribute of the event device. The attribute name may address another device with the [SUBSYSTEM/KERNEL]attribute format (see Referring to Other Devices above), and a /*/ sequence in it is expanded as described for TEST above. The assigned value supports string substitutions; see String Substitutions below.
The value that should be written to kernel parameter. The parameter name and the assigned value support string substitutions; see String Substitutions below.

Specify a program to be executed after processing of all the rules for the event. With +=, this invocation is added to the list, and with = or :=, it replaces any previous contents of the list. Please note that both program and builtin types described below share a common list, so clearing the list with := and = affects both types.
type may be:
Execute an external program specified as the assigned value.
This is the default if no type is specified.
As program, but use one of the built-in programs rather than an external one.
How the command line is specified, and which restrictions apply to the executed program, are described in Program Execution below.
A named label to which a GOTO may jump.
Jumps to the next LABEL with a matching name. The label must appear later in the same rules file; a GOTO without a matching label is ignored.
Import a set of variables as device properties, depending on type:

Execute an external program specified as the assigned value and, if it returns successfully, import its output, which must be in environment key format. How the command line is specified, and which restrictions apply to the executed program, are described in Program Execution below. If the value matches the name of a built-in program, the built-in is executed instead.
Similar to program, but use one of the built-in programs rather than an external one.
Import a text file specified as the assigned value, the content of which must be in environment key format.
Import a single property specified as the assigned value from the current device database. This works only if the database is already populated by an earlier event.
Import a single property from the kernel command line. For simple flags the value of the property is set to 1.

Import the stored keys from the parent device by reading the database entry of the parent device. The value assigned to IMPORT{parent} is used as a filter of key names to import (with the same shell glob pattern matching used for comparisons). Unlike match values, this pattern does not support alternate patterns separated by |.
Note that multiple IMPORT{} keys may be specified in one rule. The key is true if the import is successful, unless != is used as the operator which causes the key to be true if the import failed.
Rule and device options:
Specify the priority of the created symlinks. Devices with higher priorities overwrite existing symlinks of other devices. The default is 0.

When replace, possibly unsafe characters in strings assigned to NAME, SYMLINK, and ENV{key} are replaced. When none, no replacement is performed. When unset, the replacement is performed for NAME, SYMLINK, but not for ENV{key}. Defaults to unset.

Apply the permissions specified in this rule to the static device node with the specified name. Also, for every tag specified in this rule, create a symlink in the directory /run/udev/static_node-tags/tag pointing at the static device node with the specified name. Static device node creation is performed by systemd-tmpfiles before systemd-udevd is started. The static nodes might not have a corresponding kernel device; they are used to trigger automatic kernel module loading when they are accessed.
Watch the device node; when the node is closed after being opened for writing, a change uevent is synthesized.
Disable the watching of a device node.

Set the flag (sticky bit) on the udev database entry of the event device. Device properties are then kept in the database even when udevadm info --cleanup-db is called. This option can be useful in certain cases (e.g. Device Mapper devices) for persisting device state on the transition from initrd.

Takes a log level name like debug or info, or a special value reset. When a log level name is specified, the maximum log level is changed to that level. When reset is set, then the previously specified log level is revoked. Defaults to the log level of the main process of systemd-udevd.

This may be useful when debugging events for certain devices. Note that the log level is applied when the line including this rule is processed. So, for debugging, it is recommended that this is specified at earlier place, e.g., the first line of 00-debug.rules. For an example, see the Examples section below.
Dump the status of the event currently processing. It may be useful for debugging udev rules by inserting this option.
Similar to dump, but dump the status of the event in JSON format.

refsect1.title: Program Execution
refsect1.para: The PROGRAM and IMPORT{program} match keys and the RUN{program} assignment key execute external programs as part of the event processing. (The IMPORT{builtin} and RUN{builtin} variants use built-in programs instead; see IMPORT{} and RUN{} above.)

The program name and following arguments are separated by spaces. Single quotes can be used to specify arguments with spaces. If no absolute path is given, the program is expected to live in /usr/lib/udev; otherwise, the absolute path must be specified.
The device properties are made available to the executed program in the environment.
Program execution can only be used for very short-running foreground tasks. Running an event process for a long period of time may block all further events for this or a dependent device.
Note that running programs that access the network or mount/unmount filesystems is not allowed inside of udev rules, due to the default sandbox that is enforced on systemd-udevd.service.

Starting daemons or other long-running processes is not allowed; the forked processes, detached or not, will be unconditionally killed after the event handling has finished. In order to activate long-running processes from udev rules, provide a service unit and pull it in from a udev device using the SYSTEMD_WANTS device property. See systemd.device5 for details.

refsect1.title: String Substitutions
refsect1.para: Values (and, for some keys, attribute names) may contain references to device properties and other data, which are replaced when the rule is processed. Substitutions are applied to the values of the ENV, GROUP, MODE, NAME, OWNER, RUN, SECLABEL, SYMLINK, TAG and ATTR/SYSCTL assignment keys, to the values of the TEST, PROGRAM and IMPORT{file}, IMPORT{program}, IMPORT{builtin} and IMPORT{parent} match keys, and to the attribute names of the ATTR and ATTRS match keys and the SYSCTL key.

Substitutions are performed while the individual rule is being processed: values of RUN are substituted when the rule is processed (and the result is executed later, after all rules have been processed), so device properties set by earlier rules can be used, but properties set by later rules cannot. Which properties of the same rule are visible depends on the token processing order; see Token Processing Order above. The values of the other match keys are not substituted: for example, KERNEL=="%k" matches the literal string %k.
The available substitutions are:

listitem.para: The kernel name for this device.
The kernel number for this device. For example, sda3 has kernel number 3. It is empty if the kernel name does not end in digits.
The devpath of the device.
The kernel name of the device matched while searching the devpath upwards for SUBSYSTEMS, KERNELS, DRIVERS, and ATTRS.
The driver name of the device matched while searching the devpath upwards for SUBSYSTEMS, KERNELS, DRIVERS, and ATTRS.

The value of a sysfs attribute found at the device where all keys of the rule have matched. If the matching device does not have such an attribute, and a previous KERNELS, SUBSYSTEMS, DRIVERS, or ATTRS test selected a parent device, then the attribute from that parent device is used.
The attribute may also address another device with the [SUBSYSTEM/KERNEL]attribute format; see Referring to Other Devices above.
If the attribute is a symlink, the last element of the symlink target is returned as the value.
A device property value.
The kernel major number for the device.
The kernel minor number for the device.

The string returned by the external program requested with PROGRAM. A single part of the string, separated by a space character, may be selected by specifying the part number as an attribute: %c{N}. If the number is followed by the + character, this part plus all remaining parts of the result string are substituted: %c{N+}.
The node name of the parent device.
The current name of the device. If not changed by a rule, it is the name of the kernel device.
A space-separated list of the current symlinks. The value is only set during a remove event or if an earlier rule assigned a value.
The udev_root value.
The sysfs mount point.
The name of the device node.
A deprecated alias for $devnode.
A deprecated alias for $attr{file}.
The % character itself.
The $ character itself.

refsect1.title: Event Actions
refsect1.para: The ACTION match key tests the action that triggered the uevent. Uevents originate from the kernel; the following actions are processed by udev:

row.entry: A device has been created or initialized.
A device is being removed; see below.

A device has changed its state or properties; the device node is kept, but rules are re-run and symlinks and permissions are re-created. udev itself synthesizes change events in some cases, e.g. for the watch option.
A device has been moved or renamed; the previous devpath is available in the DEVPATH_OLD property.
A device has been set online.
A device has been set offline.
A device driver has been bound to the device.
A device driver has been unbound from the device.

refsect1.para: Which events are emitted, and when, is subsystem-specific; see the kernel documentation of the kobject infrastructure for background. When a device is removed, the kernel emits a remove event for each device of the affected hierarchy (e.g. for each partition before the containing disk), after the device node itself (such as /dev/sda1) has already been removed. Symlinks created by udev do not cause separate events; they are cleaned up by udev when the corresponding remove event is processed.

When a remove event is processed, the device properties stored by earlier events are first read into memory and remain available for matching, and the $links substitution expands to the symlinks that were created for the device. Before the rules are processed, systemd-udevd already removes the tag index entries and the database entry of the device; the symlinks it created are removed after the rules have been processed. Assignments that manage the device node (NAME, SYMLINK, OWNER, GROUP, MODE) have no effect.

refsect1.title: Authoring and Debugging Rules
refsect1.para: To write a rule that matches a specific device, first find out which values are available to match against. The udevadm8 tool provides several modes for this:

listitem.para: udevadm info --query=all device shows the properties, device node name and symlinks of a device, i.e. the values tested by the ENV, KERNEL, DEVPATH and SYMLINK keys.

udevadm info --attribute-walk device shows the device chain — for the event device and each of its parents, the values tested by the KERNELS, SUBSYSTEMS, DRIVERS and ATTRS keys are listed in order. This is the primary tool for writing parent device matches: a rule that combines several parent match keys must match them all at one of the devices shown.
udevadm monitor shows uevents as they arrive, including the action and devpath, while devices are (dis)connected or change state.

refsect1.para: Rules can be tested before they are installed:

listitem.para: udevadm verify checks rules files for syntax errors and common mistakes (such as duplicate or conflicting expressions).

udevadm test --action=action devpath processes all rules against a device without applying changes — device nodes, symlinks and the database are not modified, and programs specified with RUN are not executed — showing which rules match and what would be assigned. Of the programs invoked by the PROGRAM and IMPORT{program} keys, only a few well-known helpers (ata_id, cdrom_id, dmi_memory_id, fido_id, mtd_probe and scsi_id) are actually executed; other commands are skipped and reported as successful with empty output.

refsect1.para: For events processed by the running daemon, the log_level= and dump options (see OPTIONS above) can be used to inspect the processing of specific devices. Detailed per-token tracing — log messages for every token that passes, fails, or is applied — is enabled with udevadm control --trace=yes, which also raises the log level to debug (as does the udev.trace=1 kernel command line option), or shown by udevadm test --verbose.

For devices identified by their hardware properties, the hardware database described in systemd-hwdb8 provides an alternative to udev rules: it maps modalias-style match keys to device properties, which can be imported into the event with IMPORT{builtin}="hwdb" and then matched with the ENV key.

example.title: Import properties and use them in later rules
example.para: For a partition, the properties of the containing disk (stored in its database entry during an earlier event) are imported from the parent device. As IMPORT runs after the plain match keys, the imported properties are matched in a second rule, where they are also available to the SYMLINK assignment:
example.programlisting: SUBSYSTEM=="block", ENV{DEVTYPE}=="partition", IMPORT{parent}=="ID_*" SUBSYSTEM=="block", ENV{DEVTYPE}=="partition", ENV{ID_SERIAL}=="?*", \ SYMLINK+="disk-by-serial-$env{ID_SERIAL}-part$number"

example.title: Skip parts of a rules file
example.programlisting: # Network interface rules follow; skip everything else. SUBSYSTEM!="net", GOTO="net_end" ATTR{address}=="52:54:00:12:34:56", NAME="lan0" LABEL="net_end"
